 Student groups condemn Cabinet over dropping promised 2.5 % student-loan interest cap 
 Saturday, 24 October 2026 - 12:15
 Student groups reacted with anger after the Dutch Cabinet said it cannot afford the 2.5 percent interest-rate ceiling on student loans it had promised. The Dutch Student Union (LSVb) said students are being “kicked into adult life carrying a backbreaking backpack,” while the Dutch National Students Association (ISO) added that the coalition leaves students once again “the victims of empty promises.”
 At the start of the Jetten Cabinet, D66, VVD, and CDA agreed that former students would pay a maximum 2.5 percent interest on their loans. The measure was intended to protect young adults from sudden interest-rate spikes.
 It has now become apparent that the Cabinet underestimated the cost of the policy. The 40-million euros set aside are not enough to keep the interest rates artificially low. Geopolitical tensions are reportedly also driving up rates so sharply that roughly three times as much money would most likely be required.
 Additionally, next year, the interest rate for most students will rise to 2.7 percent, according to the student-loan agency Duo. This marks the first time the rate has risen above 2.5 percent, while the rate is expected to climb even further to 3.3 percent or more in the years ahead. Before 2023, for example, the rate was zero for a long period of time.
 “Students are being kicked into adult life carrying a backbreaking backpack,” the LSVb argued. “The interest-rate ceiling was the only ray of light at the end of a long, dark tunnel. The only certainty this Cabinet is willing to give students is the certainty that interest rates will keep rising in the coming years.”
 The Dutch National Students Association (ISO) is also disappointed. “The coalition made a promise it now cannot keep. Students are once again the victims of empty promises,” it said.
 Earlier this month, Statistics Netherlands (CBS) figures showed that total student debt in the Netherlands had declined for the first time. In the meantime, the number of people with large debts of 50,000 euros or higher rose to 145,000.
 D66 Minister Letschert has suggested possible solutions, including a fixed “interest discount” of about 0.2 percentage points. But the promised 40 million euros are almost certainly insufficient for “a substantial measure that would actually help (former) students.”
